transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-22
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~40 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Ava Li (Redwood CSM), Marta Gomez (BrightLayer CTO), Eli Turner (BrightLayer ML Eng), Priya Shah (BrightLayer Infra), Samir Desai (BrightLayer Product)

Summary: Weekly POC sync focused on caching (prefix & KV), observed hit rates, prompt reuse strategy, and next tuning steps. We reviewed the latest 24h benchmark, discussed TTL adjustments, concerns about caching PHI, and agreed on a 48h extended run plus instrumentation tasks.

[00:00] Sofia: Hey folks, good morning, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then we'll jump into the 24-hour results.
[00:12] Marta: Morning. All good here.
[00:15] Eli: Morning. Ready to go.
[00:18] Daniel: Hi everyone. I'll share my screen in a sec to walk through the metric dashboard.
[00:30] Daniel: Okay sharing. So this is the prefix cache overview - note that our test ran with prefix TTL = 600s and KV cache enabled for conversation state.
[00:45] Priya: Quick question, when you say KV cache enabled, that's the short-lived in-memory KV cache on the GPU node vs like a long term store, right?
[00:57] Daniel: Yeah, exactly. It's the local KV cache keeping decoded key/value states to speed up repeated prefixes; it doesn't persist across node restarts in this config.
[01:10] Marta: Got it. Can you show the hit rate numbers?
[01:15] Daniel: Sure. For the 24h run, overall prefix hit rate across the pilot routes was 46% - but that's a weighted number. Some high-reuse routes are up at ~78%, low-reuse ones down at ~12%. KV cache hit (per-token) was about 31% overall.
[01:35] Eli: Huh, the KV percent seems low relative to prefix. Are we seeing many partial matches or token misalignment causing misses?
[01:42] Daniel: Good call. We dug into that - a lot of misses are due to minor prompt variations: timestamp strings, user IDs embedded in prompts, and some small templating differences. So the prefix system can match longer fixed sequences, but when templates change we drop to partial or zero hits.
[02:05] Sofia: That's where prompt reuse strategy comes in - canonicalization, hashing stable slots, or using placeholders.
[02:12] Samir: We can probably standardize some of the product messages; our UX team injects per-user IDs for analytics so that explains a chunk.
[02:22] Priya: Also, are we redacting anything before caching? Anything PII or PHI? We are regulated, so can't cache raw PHI.
[02:32] Daniel: We flagged that in the config - for pilot we masked obvious IDs via a pre-processing step, but we need to formalize the redaction rules before widening cache. Right now the cache is configured to bypass when the redaction flag is set.
[02:45] Marta: Good. Please put that in an action item.
[02:50] Ava: noted.
[02:55] Daniel: Back to numbers - route A (patient-summarization flow) had prefix hits of 72% and KV hits of 54%. Route B (triage chat) had prefix 18% and KV 9%. Route C (billing FAQ) very high reuse, prefix 88%, KV 66%.
[03:20] Eli: Billing makes sense - static templates. Triage is the free-text area so less reuse.
[03:30] Daniel: We experimented with two TTL configs: 600s and 300s. Shorter TTL reduced stale matches but slightly decreased overall byte-saved efficiency. With 300s, weighted prefix hit dropped 4 points but KV stayed similar.
[03:48] Sofia: So tradeoff is freshness vs cache utility. For triage we'd accept lower TTLs; for billing use longer TTL.
[03:57] Marta: Makes sense. What's the impact on latency?
[04:00] Daniel: For high-hit routes, 95p latency improved by ~110ms; p50 improved ~35ms. For low-hit routes negligible.
[04:12] Eli: Can we route traffic so high-value flows use dedicated instances to preserve cache locality?
[04:18] Sofia: Yes, routing by route or customer segment is supported; we can pin those flows to dedicated pools or at minimum ensure affinity to same node pool.
[04:28] Priya: Any concerns about cache warm-up after deploys or scaling events? We saw a spike last Tuesday when nodes cycled.
[04:36] Daniel: Node churn will flush local KV cache; we can mitigate with slower rollouts and sticky routing. We also have a persistent LRU-backed microcache option to rehydrate frequent prefixes, but that adds complexity and slightly higher memory footprint.
[04:52] Marta: How big is the memory hit? Could you quantify?
[04:56] Daniel: Rough ballpark: for our pilot traffic, enabling persistent microcache added ~1.2GB per node for top-500 prefixes. We can tune size.
[05:06] Samir: If memory is acceptable we could pilot microcache on billing and patient-summary only.
[05:12] Sofia: OK noted. Next up, prompt canonicalization. Eli, you mentioned you have examples?
[05:17] Eli: Yeah I shared a small set in the repo. The problem is the front-end injects timestamps like '<TS> 2025-04-22T09:...' and session IDs. We can replace those with tokens like <TS> and <SID> before hashing.
[05:30] Daniel: Exactly - we recommend a two-layer canonicalization: structural placeholders + normalization (lowercase, strip punctuation in certain slots) then compute prefix hash for cache lookup.
[05:43] Priya: Does that affect model outputs? If we canonicalize too aggressively we might lose user-specific context.
[05:49] Daniel: We apply canonicalization only for the cache key derivation; the request forwarded to the model retains the full original prompt. So it's safe.
[05:59] Marta: Good. Any ETA on tooling?
[06:02] Daniel: I can push a small library and an example middleware by end of week.
[06:07] Sofia: That would help.
[06:10] [10:06] 
[06:12] Daniel: On the benchmarking side, we ran a 'cold' vs 'warmed' comparison. Cold (empty cache) throughput was baseline, warmed was +27% throughput and token cost down ~18% due to fewer decode steps.
[06:30] Eli: Nice. How reproducible is that?
[06:33] Daniel: For high-reuse routes it's stable; for low-reuse it varies more. We're proposing a 48-hour extended run to get a stable distribution through different traffic patterns.
[06:45] Marta: Let's do that. Sofia, can Redwood kick that off?
[06:48] Sofia: Yes we can. We'll run it starting tomorrow and share the CSV and dashboards.
[06:54] Priya: Also, we need more granular per-user hit-rate rolling window. Right now it's aggregated; we want per-route and per-tenant.
[07:04] Daniel: I'll wire per-tenant panels. That will show skew - some tenants have 80% reuse while others 5%.
[07:12] Samir: Could we also log anonymized examples of prefix hits/misses so we can tune canonicalization?
[07:18] Daniel: We can emit hashed samples and a truncated prompt snapshot with identifiers removed. Avoid logging PHI.
[07:26] Priya: Important: for any example logs we must pass compliance review first.
[07:30] Ava: adding that to action items.
[07:34] [20:00] 
[07:36] Marta: On the security front, what about encryption of cache in memory and at rest?
[07:40] Daniel: The in-memory cache is on the node and not persisted to disk in the default pilot. Node memory is ephemeral. For private deployments we can leverage KMS wrapped keys for any persisted microcache and ensure encryption at rest.
[07:54] Priya: Ok, good. Please include architecture notes.
[07:57] Daniel: Will do.
[08:00] Eli: Quick thought - could we use a short-lived per-session salt in the hash to avoid cross-tenant collisions?
[08:08] Daniel: We can namespace cache keys by tenant id, which is simpler. Per-session salt would reduce cacheability across sessions so not ideal.
[08:18] Sofia: Let's namespace by tenant + route for now.
[08:22] Marta: Agreed.
[08:24] [30:00] 
[08:26] Daniel: Final recommended changes from Redwood: 1) implement canonicalization middleware (placeholders for timestamps/IDs), 2) TTL per-route (billing 1800s, patient-summary 1200s, triage 300s), 3) pilot microcache on high-reuse routes, 4) run 48h extended benchmark, 5) dashboard per-tenant hit rates and anonymized sample logging.
[08:52] Eli: That aligns with our priorities.
[08:55] Priya: A couple implementation questions - will canonicalization run at the edge or in your control plane?
[09:02] Daniel: For the pilot we propose middleware in the customer calling path (edge) so you control the redaction rules; Redwood provides the reference library and pattern. For Private deployments we can help with rollout.
[09:16] Marta: Good. Any blockers on Redwood side?
[09:19] Sofia: None - we'll need your prompt families and the compliance checklist for redaction.
[09:24] Marta: We'll get that over.
[09:28] Sofia: Great. Recap of next steps: Redwood runs 48h benchmark (Sofia/Daniel), Daniel adds dashboard panels and shares config snippets, BrightLayer sends prompt examples and redaction requirements (Eli/Priya), security review scheduled.
[09:45] Ava: I'll capture and follow up with calendar invites.
[09:50] Marta: Thanks everyone.
[09:52] Sofia: Thanks, we'll follow up with the report tomorrow.
[09:55] Meeting end.
